newsitem.title: USA: AFL-CIO chief criticizes balanced budget amendment.
newsitem.headline: AFL-CIO chief criticizes balanced budget amendment.

text.p: AFL-CIO President John Sweeney spoke out against a proposed balanced budget amendment Friday, calling it a reckless ploy to cut services and protections for working families.
The 78 unions of the AFL-CIO represent 13.1 million workers.

In a speech to the Commonwealth Club of California, the labour leader said America's wage and wealth gap, the balanced budget amendment plan and proposals to privatise Social Security "make up a devil's brew for our economy and for our country."

Sweeney opposed the Republican-backed plan for a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution, calling it "a reckless, indefensible ploy to cut the services and programmes and protections working families depend upon most."

He likened the proposal, now before Congress, to "putting our country in an economic straitjacket that would prevent federal borrowing to finance any sort of infrastructure, much less a bridge to a new century."
He described proposals to privatise Social Security as "another way to fool around recklessly" with the economy.

An advisory panel set up to suggest ways to ensure the long-term health of Social Security issued conflicting plans last month. But the panel agreed that some of the program's billions of dollars in payroll taxes should be invested in private financial markets.

"Now I really am tempted to ask... how smart it is to invest our future in a bull market being fuelled by the savings of Baby Boomers who in 30 years, just when we need the money most, are going to be pulling all that dough out of the market," Sweeney said.
Sweeney also lamented the growing wage and wealth gap in the United States, saying that, by 1992, the richest 20 percent controlled 80 percent of the wealth.
"American workers are running out of money, running out of options and running out of hope," he said.

He said he was convinced that at some point the United States would face even harsher consequences from "the reckless pursuit of lower and lower wages by American business. People who don't have money can't spend money and that can be disastrous for an economy historically driven by optimism and consumer purchases."

Sweeney said that, working together, business and labour leaders could find ways to preserve Social Security, balance demands for government services against people's willingness to pay for them and create a new high-wage economy.
